The second meeting of the Disarmament and International Security Committee, the first committee of the 80th session of the General Assembly, is called to order. Distinguished delegates, I would like to warmly welcome all delegations to this meeting. I would like to extend a particular warm welcome to the President of the General Assembly, Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock, and the Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, Ms. Izumi Nakamitsu. In accordance with our programme of work and timetable, the Committee will begin its general debate today on all disarmament and international security agenda items allocated to it. items 19 to 106. Before we proceed, please allow me to make a brief statement in my capacity as the chair of the first committee for this session. This year marks the 80th anniversary of the atomic tragedy in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, a recurrence that should give us an even stronger impulse to promote disarmament and non-proliferation. I'm aware of the very delicate current international context characterized by ongoing conflicts and tensions requiring an even stronger architecture of global security. New challenges such as the artificial intelligence are also calling the international community to take action in order to avoid possible risks and reap the benefits associated to these emerging technologies. The task before us is not easy. States' perceptions of security often diverge profoundly, but we cannot resign ourselves to sterile multilateralism defined by opposing positions. We must instead recognize that beyond our differences lies a higher good that unites us, collective security without which no nation can truly prosper. In the current context of growing military spending worldwide, it is indeed crucial not to divert and hopefully to increase essential resources allocated to alleviate poverty and reduce alarming inequality rates within and among states in full compliance with sustainable development goals of the United Nations Agenda 2030. The multilateral methods with the UN at its core allowed to reach extremely important agreements on disarmament, such as the treaty banning nuclear tests in atmosphere, in outer space and underwater, the treaty on non-proliferation and nuclear weapons, the convention on the prohibition of the development, production and stockpiling of bacteriological and toxin weapons and on other destruction. the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, aiming for the total ban on nuclear weapons testing. This year's first committee takes place in a very important moment, being the last occasion of debate on nuclear disarmament before the review conference on the Treaty of Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons from 27 April to 22 May 2026 in New York. Another fundamental objective of the First Committee is to pursue a world free from chemical and biological weapons and ensure that those responsible for any use of these weapons are identified and held accountable. strengthen measures to prevent the acquisition of weapons of mass destruction by non-state actors. This year we also celebrate the 50th anniversary of the entry into force of the Biological Weapons Convention, an international treaty that prohibits the development, production, acquisition, stockpiling and use of biological and toxin weapons. The first committee plays an important role on conventional weapons in order to strengthen our effort to implement our respective obligations under relevant international instruments to prohibit or restrict conventional weapons due to their humanitarian impact. Reflecting the significant divisions within the international community on these issues, Around two thirds of resolutions are usually approved by vote and remaining by consensus. These numbers make us reflect on the need to work together to build consensus. Over the years, efforts have been made to improve the work of the committee, fostering efficiency and streamlining processes, avoiding duplications and overlapping. I also acknowledge that during the meeting on working methods of the first committee, A significant support emerged among Member States to consider to review the periodicity of those resolutions that are currently approved annually without or with only technical updates, if accepted by the relevant penholders and without setting a precedent. In conclusion, I would like to ensure that I will spend efforts to foster constructive engagement and ensure the full and smooth functioning of the committee with an inclusive, pragmatic and forward-looking approach aimed at revitalizing the disarmament agenda, not as an abstract goal, but as a shared imperative for international peace and security. And I thank you for all your attention. I now invite the President of the General Assembly, Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock, to address the Committee. You have the floor.

First of all, congratulations, and also congratulations to the Bureau members on the elections to lead the first Committee during the 80th session. Good morning to you, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, especially to those PRs not being based in New York, with whom I had the chance already to engage intensively, but being here from Geneva, and also very warm welcome to the experts and directors from capitals. I wish you, I wish all of us success in the work ahead after we have finished, I would say quite successfully, given the situation of our world, the high level week, now the real work, the committee season starts. And you assume this responsibility at a moment of urgency, as we all know, as conflicts devastate communities in Haiti, Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza, and so many more forgotten crises. while our commitment to disarmament and the cause of peace is visibly weakening. Due to that or besides that, people are challenging our institution, which was built for peace. So therefore, the work of this committee becomes more important, but also more challenging. I underlined in my opening remarks of the High Level Week that we have to make clear in all these debates that while the Charter is being violated from different actors and parts of the world, this is not the UN as such which is failing. Yet, we are in the world of today, and while we speak of peace, some actions and how we allocate resources tell another story. Last year, the world spent $3,169 every second on nuclear weapons. So now, now, now, now, now, $3,000 every second. Resources that were by that not used for building schools, expanding health care, and strengthening infrastructure, but instead invested in weapons capable of annihilating humanity as such. While we mark the first anniversary of the Pact for the Future, in which member states pledged to strengthen the disarmament and non-proliferation architecture, we are also seeing that that very architecture painstakingly built over decades is now being challenged from some openly, from others more from the back.

Therefore.

At this start of our working session and as the working groups evolve into the nitty-gritty substance, I think it's very important taking a realistic view of the world as it is. We must consider how we can and should work together for the future so that the hard-won successes of the past are not eroded. So our commitments during High Level Week on disarmament must not fade into rhetoric. They must live in practice here in the work of the committees, but also obviously in capitals around the world. Too many states have set aside their obligations instead of reinforcing them. Some have chosen a different path altogether. So it's our collective duty to preserve, strengthen, and update these commitments to meet new realities, especially as emerging technologies from artificial intelligence to cyber capabilities reshape our security landscape. And because I'm always believing that in international law, you have to have an optimistic view, even if the glass is not even half full, but empty, we should also consider that these kind of new topics also raise a new attention for people, for younger generations. So the outer space disarmament topics, for example, is something which could also engage totally new actors from all around the world. That will be a defining moment to recommit not only to the disarmament and non-proliferation, but to the very raison d'etre of the charter, a new commitment to peace. As we have seen also over the high-level week, but as you know also from the last years, obviously this will not be easy at all. And therefore, I would like to turn to a second point, also my capacity here now speaking not as a disarmament expert, but the PGA, that obviously the work of the working groups of the committee sessions is highly connected to the UN aid reform, so the reform agenda of the United Nations as such. I said therefore in my opening speech at the high level week that this is not an ordinary session, not for capitals, not for the General Assembly, and therefore also not for the committee work. And again, as there are also some PRs from Geneva and directors and experts from the capital here in the room, we are taking this task of UNAD reform very, very serious because we know that it's more than a reform. It's the definition of the United Nations for the next decades, for the next future. So while we are standing at a crossroads, everything we are doing here, every failure, but also every success in the committee is also being seen of strong the United Nations is as such. And therefore, coming again to the nitty-gritty part of committee work, every resolution, every working method matters, because we have to make this institution fit for the future, fit for purpose, and therefore it has to be more agile. So I would like to encourage you, when you debate the very important contact of every resolution on disarmament, on outer space, to always ask yourself, is it still making sense 80 years, 50 years later? Is this really the reality we are living in? And if we still need it-- and in your topics, most of the time, it's the DNA of this institution, peace and security. So therefore, our work in these times is not only looking at the thematic contents, but also if we can actually deliver in practice. So therefore, the UNAD initiative and the broader reform process is also about reducing text, not as a cost-cutting exercise for cost-cutting, but to make our work less bureaucratic and more efficient. I thank the President of the General Assembly for her statement. I understand that the President of the General Assembly has to leave at this time due to another engagement. We thank her once again for her presence today and we look forward to a great collaboration for the current session. Thank you very much. I have now the pleasure of inviting the Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, Ms. Izumi Nakamitsu, to make a statement. You have the floor.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Your Excellency, Ambassador Mauricio Massari, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Allow me to start by warmly congratulating Ambassador Massari on his election, as well as the members of the Bureau. I wish you success for this session. I also express deep appreciation to Ambassador Marisa Chanda Berbe of Costa Rica for her exemplary and skillful leadership during the 79th session. Our steadfast commitment to gender equality also deserves particular recognition. Women's full, equal, meaningful and effective participation in disarmament discussions is a key part of ensuring their outcomes respond to the challenges of today and, of course, the future. Distinguished delegates, I am honored to address the 80th session of the First Committee. This is the ninth time I have had this opportunity over the course of my tenure as High Representative for Disarmament Affairs. Over those nine years, there have been inevitable peaks and valleys. We have welcomed the adoption of new treaties, normative frameworks, and consensus outcome documents. Many of these successful initiatives have emanated from this very room. At the same time, there is an increasing and urgent need to confront the sobering realities of our times. The international security landscape has suffered and continues to suffer serious shocks from intensifying conflicts to rising nuclear rhetoric, to the rapid emergence of new weapons technologies. It is against this backdrop that I cannot help but offer a very candid analysis of the state of the world. I will be blunt. It is a difficult time for disarmament, international security, and also the United Nations. In 2024, global military expenditure reached a staggering 2.7 trillion US dollars. We continue to witness nuclear posturing, qualitative nuclear arms racing, and quantitative arsenal expansion. Advances in technology, particularly artificial intelligence, are far outpacing governance efforts, raising legal, security, and ethical concerns. In conflicts across regions, the devastating human cost of weapons is glaring, from the use of explosive weapons in populated areas to illicit flows of small arms and light weapons. At a time when civilians are facing heightened risks, The very frameworks in place to protect human life and dignity, such as the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention and Convention Cluster Munitions, are under serious pressure. As we face challenges on all these fronts, we must consider the capacity of the United Nations itself to respond to them. On its 80th anniversary, the United Nations relevance, effectiveness and legitimacy are especially under the spotlight. These challenges are compounded by a financial and liquidity crisis that are straining the organization's capacities to its limits. The United Nations has been forced to scale back operations at a time when they are needed the most. In response, The Secretary-General has launched the UN 80 initiative. The goal is to transform the UN into a more agile, integrated and effective organization equipped to respond to today's global challenges while also responding to budgetary pressures. The initiative seeks to streamline mandates and operations, find deficiencies and prevent duplication. The sector general has been clear that the United Nations remains the essential one-of-a-kind platform to advance peace, sustainable development, humanitarian action and human rights, a sentiment supported by a vast majority of member states. To maintain its central role in multilateralism, We must ensure the organization is fit for purpose. UNAT is a way to bring the UN up to speed. Across the Secretariat, alongside a revised budgetary process which will help us align with the current financial climate, we are undertaking broad mitigation measures to respond to the availability of significantly fewer resources. Our work in disarmament is not immune to this tightening. The Office for Disarmament Affairs has had to make very difficult decisions for more efficient utilization of fewer financial and human resources. And we will continue to strive to align our shrinking capacities with the growing needs for disarmament. But let me be clear, the secretariat would not be able to deliver the same for less. This is simply not possible. I ask Member States to carefully review any new mandate in light of available resources and capacities. While budgetary matters fall outside the purview of the First Committee, We should all be clear-eyed regarding potential substantive impacts resulting from the dual crisis of liquidity and budget. Distinguished delegates, allow me now to strike a more positive tone. Neither the United Nations as a whole, nor the Office for Disarmament Affairs specifically, will shy away from the challenges of the moment. Quite the opposite. Current institutional challenges and international security trends should rather spark renewed commitment to the enduring value of disarmament. Disarmament has always been central to the UN's foundation. From the General Assembly's very first resolution calling for the elimination of atomic weapons, to the latest initiatives tackling the international security implications of new technologies, disarmament has been a constant in these halls. My office remains your steadfast partner in ensuring this work continues, from managing biorisks to preventing an arms race in outer space to combating the re-emergence of chemical weapons. Distinguished delegates, I will now highlight a few key substantive issues with particular emphasis on opportunities I see for tackling them. In the interest of time, I will refrain from providing an exhaustive overview of all issues under the purview of the committee, but please rest assured, my office will remain fully seized of the committee's agenda. First, regarding nuclear weapons. Just last month, I visited Hiroshima and Nagasaki to mark 80 years since the devastation of atomic bombings. While the vast majority of the world continues to actively pursue the total elimination of nuclear weapons, we must do more and do it urgently. We must lower the potential temperature, political temperature, if we are to prevent nuclear war or any use of nuclear weapons. Measures to reduce risk are not substitute for disarmament, but necessary to ensure that we collectively are around long enough to achieve it. Next, we must ensure that arms control frameworks are protected. Pending the negotiation of a successor, at a minimum, Central limits on New START must be maintained. And finally, we must strengthen the nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime grounded in the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It goes without saying, a successful outcome at the 2026 NPT Review Conference is essential. Establishing a Middle East zone free of nuclear and all other weapons of mass destruction will contribute meaningfully to realizing a world free of nuclear weapons and to promoting peaceful peace and security in the Middle East and beyond. Maintaining momentum through the dedicated conference process remains crucial. Second, rising global military expenditure. Just a few weeks ago, the sector general launched a new report security we need rebalancing military spending for sustainable and peaceful future mandated by your part for the future as the Secretary General notes while global military spending source progress on the sustainable development goals is faltering with only one in five targets on track for 2030. This troubling imbalance invites us to fundamentally rethink the relationship between security, disarmament and development. We must look holistically peace and development agendas and recalibrate global financial priorities. Investment in disarmament and arms control is a direct investment in long-term peace and security and therefore sustainable development. I was heartened to hear so many heads of state and government raise concerns on rising military expenditure during the general debate of the General Assembly. This is indicative of the high level growing awareness and concern over arms racing and associated opportunity cost for achieving the SDGs. I also welcome the achievements made in the framework of the Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons, in particular the consensus outcome of the fourth review conference. At the regional level, new roadmaps and normative initiatives are helping to address the transnational nature of illicit small arms. Such developments support a solid pathway forward. that anchors regional approaches to international frameworks. Let us seize this momentum and continue to bring military expenditure to the forefront of disarmament discussions and improve linkages between arms control and development. Third, let me say a few words on emerging technologies. here, the distinct sense of urgency is unmistakable. The cutting edge technologies of today are obsolete tomorrow. And when applied in the military domain, technology, technological challenges are even more acute. Rapidly advancing technologies have the potential to revolutionize conflict dynamics in the long, not too distant future. In fact, Some already are doing so. Information and communications technologies are being used in direct connection to active hostilities. Recent conflicts have become alarming testing grounds for AI applications. And current conflicts have been a significant catalyst for accelerating the development and proliferation of armed uncrewed aerial vehicles, UAVs, from greater integration of autonomy to dramatically lower cost. Frameworks tackling dual use technologies like ICTs and AI often fall short in effectively managing their rapid proliferation and potential misuse across civilian and military domains. That said, we have seen concrete movement forward at the UN in some of those areas. demonstrating that even amid deepening geopolitical divide and growing mistrust, progress on critical and urgent issues is still possible. The consensus establishment of a new permanent global mechanism on ICT security set to begin its work in 2026 is a case in point. I also welcome the progress made this year in advancing discussions on lethal autonomous weapon systems, both within the General Assembly and in particular within the group of governmental experts of the CCW, which I hope will produce ambitious elements on concrete regulations. Fundamentally, we must ensure that human judgment and control is preserved in the use of force. As the Sector General regularly underscores, technologies must serve humanity, not the other way around. Distinguished delegates, as we found ourselves in an exceptionally difficult moment, we need new ideas, renewed energy and a dose of creativity. This is why I have always stressed the importance of engaging young people in disarmament conversations. Exactly one year ago, when I addressed this committee, I suggested the creation of a Disarmament Youth Forum. Today, I am very pleased to announce that this idea has come to fruition. My office, with the general support of the Republic of Korea, will host the first ever the UN Youth for Disarmament Forum here at headquarters from 16 to 17 October. The forum has been developed with young people, for young people, placing meaningful youth participation at the heart of its design. I invite all delegations to follow the forum in the spirit of working better together, as mentioned by the Madam President of the General Assembly, to advance our shared goals of international peace and security. The challenges we face are solvable, and the moment to act is now. Rest assured, my office is here to support all delegations to this end. I thank you very much for your attention.

Mr. Chairman, I am honored to speak on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. NAAM reaffirms its strong commitment to the purposes, principles and provisions of the Charter of the United Nations and international law. NAAM reiterates its condemnation of the ongoing Israeli aggression on Gaza, which continues to cause untold human casualties and destruction. NAAM further condemns the ongoing Israeli aggression on Lebanon, which has caused thousands of casualties and injuries among civilians, a massive wave of displacement and widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, of the systematic and complete destruction of many border villages. NAM reiterates its categorical and strong condemnation and denunciation of the wanton, unprovoked and premeditated heinous attack of Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran, perpetrated between 13th and 24th June 2025, as well as the deliberate targeting of Iran's IAEA safeguarded peaceful nuclear facilities by Israel and the United States. NAM reiterates its continued concern over current challenges in the field of disarmament and international security amid these tightened global geopolitical tensions, further necessitating the promotion and earliest achievement of nuclear disarmament goals. NAM reaffirms its principled position on nuclear disarmament. which remains the agreed highest priority for the UN in the area of disarmament in accordance with the final document of SSODI 1978. NAM states parties to the NPT reiterates the urgent need for the accountability of nuclear weapons states for their disarmament obligations under the NPT, particularly Article VI. NAM expresses deep concern at the sustained modernization of nuclear weapons, the continuous improvements in existing nuclear weapons, and the development of new types of nuclear weapons as provided for in the military doctrines of some NWS, and also calls on NWS to immediately cease their plans to further modernize, upgrade, refurbish, or extend the lives of their nuclear weapons and related facilities. NAM welcomes multilateral efforts towards nuclear disarmament and the total elimination of nuclear weapons. NAM underlines the importance and relevance of the UN Disarmament Commission with universal membership as the sole specialized and deliberative body within the UN multilateral disarmament machinery in considering various challenges in the field of disarmament and submit concrete recommendations to the GA. NAM once again renews its strong call upon NWS to fully and urgently comply with their legal obligations and unequivocal undertaking to accomplish the total elimination of their nuclear weapons without further delay in a transparent, irreversible and internationally verifiable manner. Chair, non-state parties to the NPT express their disappointment over consecutive failures of the ninth and the tenth NPT review conferences to adopt the consensus outcome document despite the constructive engagement of non-state parties to the NPT and underscores that continued failure at the 11th NPT review conference is not an option as it would undermine the credibility of the treaty. Non-state parties to the NPT emphasize the special responsibility of co-sponsor states of the 1995 resolution on the Middle East in implementation of that resolution and are concerned that the persistent lack of implementation of the 1995 resolution contrary to the decisions made at the relevant NPT review conference undermines the effectiveness and credibility of the NPT and disrupts the delicate balance between its three pillars, taking into account that the indefinite extension of the treaty agreed the 1995 review conference is inextricably linked to the implementation of 1995 resolution on the Middle East in this regard nam welcomes the convening of the five sessions of the conference on the establishment of the Middle East zone free of nuclear weapons according to the general assembly resolution decision rather 73 stroke 546 and the available deliberations and reports including most recently under the presidency of Mauritania November 2024. NAM looks forward to the convening of the sixth session of the conference under the presidency of the Kingdom of Morocco from 17th to 21st November 2025. NAM reaffirms the inalienable right of each state to develop research to the production and use of nuclear energy, including the sovereign right to develop full national nuclear fuel cycle for peaceful purposes, without discrimination. NAM once again reaffirms the sovereign right of each state to define its national energy policies. NAM stresses that any decision on multilateral approaches to nuclear fuel cycle shall be made by consensus and without prejudice to the inalienable right of each state to develop a full national nuclear fuel cycle. NAM reaffirms the continued significance of the spirit of collaboration and multilateralism that led to the unanimous adoption of Security Council Resolution 2231 of 2015 and underscores that its provisions and timeline must be strictly respected. Now further stresses that all provisions of the resolution should be terminated in accordance with paragraph eight of resolution 2231 thereof. I now call upon the Conference on Disarmament to negotiate an international agreement on the prohibition of attacks against nuclear facilities based on the previous work done in this area. I now believe that nuclear weapon-free zones, NWFZs, established by the treaties of Tlatelolco, Rarotonga, Bangkok, the Central Asian Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaty, as well as the Mongolia's nuclear weapon free status, are positive steps and important measures towards strengthening global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. NAM states, NAM reiterates its full support for the establishment of the Middle East of a zone free of nuclear weapons and all other WMDs. Chair, Namibia State parties to the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons, CWC, note with satisfaction the effective operation of the CWC as a comprehensive multilateral treaty banning an entire category of weapons of mass destruction, providing for verification system and promoting the use of chemicals for peaceful purposes. NAM states parties to the Biological Weapons Convention, BWC, consider that the convention represents an important component of the international legal architecture related to WMD. They recognize that the lack of verification system continues to pose a challenge to the effectiveness of the convention. NAM remains deeply concerned over a wide range of security, humanitarian, and socioeconomic consequences arising from the illicit manufacture, transfer, and circulation of small weapons and light weapons, SALW, which may include pursuant relevant national laws, small arms, and light weapons that are illicitly manufactured through the illicit use of additive manufactured technologies, while underlining that efforts should not hinder the legitimate use or transfer of these technologies. NAM welcomes the successful conclusion of the work of the OEWG on security of and in the use of information and communication technologies, 2021-2025, established by the UN General Assembly resolution 75/140, OEWG 2021-2025. NAM further welcomes the adoption of the OEWG final report by consensus, including the elements for the establishment of the United Nations global mechanism on the development in the field of ICTs in the context of international security and advancing responsible state behavior in the use of ICTs as the mechanism within the UN for dialogue on security of and the use of ICTs based on consensus with active and equal participation of all states. following the conclusion of the work of OEWG 2021-2025. NAM calls for ensuring a seamless transition from OEWG to UN global mechanism based on the consensus elements contained in the annex C of OEWG's third annual progress report, as well as annex one of OEWG's final report. In this regard, Chair, NAM reiterates the importance of the endorsement of the OEWG's final report by the General Assembly through a single consensus resolution tabled in the First Committee. NAM strongly emphasizes the need to reach consensus within the global mechanism in considering the remaining outstanding issues as reflected in the Chair's summary attached to the final substantive report of the 2019-2021 OEWG. now further underscores the importance of achieving meaningful progress on matters related to capacity building as well as international law. The Chairman now expresses his deep concern on the continued lack of adequate representation from NAM countries in the UN Office for Development Affairs, UNODA, and requests the Secretary General and High Representative to undertake steps to ensure proper, balanced and equitable representation in that office. NAM underscores the importance of convening SSOD IV as it would offer an opportunity to review from a perspective more in tune with the current international situation the most critical aspects of the disarmament process and mobilize the international community and public opinion in favor of the elimination of nuclear weapons. In conclusion, NAM underlines the imperative political will all parties. NAM is confident that with political courage and by working together comparatively, the first committee will contribute tangibly in building a more secure and peaceful world. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Uganda for his statement. I give now the floor to His Excellency, Permanent Representative of Guinea-Bissau on behalf of African Group.

Thank you. Mr. Chairman, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the African group. Mr. Chair, at the outset, I congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election. You can count on the group's full support and cooperation throughout this session. The African group aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. This debate comes at a time of growing global insecurity, when disarmament and non-proliferation architecture faces unprecedented strain. The African Group reaffirms that multilateral diplomacy remains the cornerstone for addressing disarmament, non-proliferation and international security challenges in line with the UN Charter and the outcomes of the first special session on disarmament. Mr. Chairman, the total elimination of nuclear weapons remains the only absolute guarantee against their use or threat of use. The continued existence and modernization of nuclear arsenals pose an existential threat to humanity. The African Group therefore calls for concrete, transparent, verifiable measures toward complete nuclear disarmament within an agreed timeframe. The Group expresses deep disappointment at the consecutive failures at the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conferences, which undermine confidence in the Treaty. We urge all States parties to renew commitment to their disarmament obligations, including implementation of the 1995 Middle East resolution and prior agreed outcomes. The African Group expresses deep concern on a threat and unfortunate statement made by an Israeli minister last October for suggesting detonation of nuclear weapons on Gaza Strip. These are shocking statements that require solemn condemnation and further reinforce the urgent necessity of a zone free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in the region as an indispensable asset for regional and international peace and security and international law. The African group reiterates the importance of nuclear weapons free zone as a practical step toward global disarmament. In this context, we reaffirm the Treaty of Pelindaba, which establishes Africa as a nuclear weapons free zone, prohibiting testing, stationing, or acquisition of nuclear explosive devices on the continent. The group also welcomes the five session of the United Nations Conference on establishing a Middle East zone free of nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction and urge all relevant states to engage constructively in this open and inclusive process. Mr. Chairman, the African Group reaffirms the inalienable right of states to the peaceful use of nuclear energy and commends the continued technical support of the International Atomic Energy Agency in promoting science and technology for sustainable development. The group attaches high importance to the treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons, which strengthens the global norm against nuclear weapons. We welcome the outcome of the third meeting of states parties in March 2025 and look forward to the first review conference under the chairmanship of South Africa. We urge all states particularly nuclear weapon states and those under nuclear umbrellas, to sign and ratify the treaty without delay. The group underscores the urgency of universal adherence to the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty and calls upon all annexed two states to ratify it so it may enter into force and reinforce the global norm against nuclear testing. The African Group attaches great importance to the work of the United Nations Disarmament Commission and the Conference on Disarmament. We call for renewed commitment to their mandates and urge the CD to adopt a balanced and comprehensive programme of work without further delay. The Group remains gravely concerned over the illicit trade and circulation of small arms and light weapons which continue to fuel conflicts in Africa. We reaffirm our commitment to the UN Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons and welcome the adoption of the outcome of the fourth review conference held in June 2025. We further commend the role of the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa. in providing technical assistance and capacity building despite limited resources. The Group appeals for greater support to enable UNOOSA to effectively fulfil its mandate. Mr. Chairman, the African Group underscores the importance of preventing an arms race in outer space through legally binding instruments that uphold the principles of peaceful use and non-appropriation of outer space. We welcome progress made by the new open-ended working group on the prevention of an arms race in outer space and call for continued inclusive dialogue. The group also attaches importance to discussions on the security of information and communication technologies and on emerging issues such as artificial intelligence and lethal autonomous weapons. We emphasize that international law applies fully in these domains and that human control and accountability must remain central to all military applications on new technology. Mr. Chairman, the African Group reiterates that political will, trust, and transparency are indispensable to progress in disarmament. We urge all states to work collectively to advance the cause of international peace and security. The African Group will table three draft resolutions on this session, namely, the African Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaty, Pelindaba, the Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa, and the prohibition of dumping of radioactive wastes. We look forward to the support of all delegations for their adoption by consensus. Thank you all.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Guinea-Bissau for his statement. I give now the floor to His Excellency the Permanent Representative of Malaysia on behalf of the Association of Southeast Asian.

Thank you, Chair. I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of ASEAN. The full version will be posted on e-Journal. In conclusion, ASEAN looks forward to constructive engagement with all delegations and stakeholders during the present session of the First Committee. Thank you.

I thank the permanent representative of Malaysia for his statement. I give now the floor to the permanent representative, His Excellency, Her Excellency, I'm sorry, of Iceland on behalf of Nordic countries.

Mr. Chair, Let me congratulate you, Ambassador Massari, and the Bureau on your election and wish you all the best in your work ahead. It's an honor to address this committee on behalf of the Nordic countries, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and my own country, Iceland. I will make a shortened version of the statement, the full version being posted on the committee's website. Let me start by underlining the pivotal importance of protecting multilateralism and promoting respect for international law. In these times of multiple military conflicts and serious challenges to global peace and security, it is more important than ever to uphold the architecture for arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation. The Nordic countries once again condemn Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine that violates the most fundamental principles of international law. We reaffirm our unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. Russia must immediately cease its war of aggression and withdraw its troops from the entire territory of Ukraine. Russia's war has had profound consequences for the security situation in Europe and beyond. In response, also the Nordic countries have had to increase our defensive capabilities. These are resources we could have used for other purposes. It is equally clear that the war in Gaza must end now. Our countries have consistently condemned the horrific terrorist attacks by Hamas two years ago, demanded the release of all hostages, and affirmed that Israel has a right to defend itself. But what we have witnessed in Gaza has gone far beyond this right. We call for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and unhindered humanitarian access. We support all efforts aimed at achieving a just and lasting peace. All parties must seize the opportunity presented by the United States peace plan and do what they can to resolve the conflict. It is crucial not to lose sight of the ultimate goal, a lasting two-state solution. These brutal wars and other active conflicts around the world not only threaten regional security but undermine global stability. We are at risk of reversing the progress achieved through decades of multilateral cooperation, including on arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation. We must intensify our efforts to sustain the frameworks we built over the past 80 years, the rule-based international order that has served to advance development and human prosperity through the principles of sovereign equality of states, prohibition of the use of force and peaceful settlement of disputes. Mr. Chair, the Nordic countries reaffirm their strong commitment to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, which remains the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation regime. The NPT is the only credible path towards nuclear disarmament and provides the foundations for international cooperation on peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology. We emphasize the importance of full implementation of the treaty's three interrelated pillars. As we approach the 2026 NPT Review Conference, we call on all state parties to work together in good faith to strengthen the treaty and advance its goals. The International Atomic Energy Agency has a key role in ensuring adherence to the NPT's obligations, and the agency's safeguard systems remain essential. The Nordic countries greatly value the professionalism, impartiality and scientific expertise of the IAEA, and we reiterate our full support for its work to promote nuclear safety and security, as well as peaceful uses of nuclear technologies. Russia's war of aggression continues to endanger nuclear safety and security in Ukraine. We condemn Russia's illegal and reckless actions and commend the efforts of the IAEA to ensure nuclear safety and security at Zaporizhzhia and other Ukrainian nuclear power plants. Developments in recent months relating to Iran's nuclear programme are of serious concern. Iran must never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon and must comply with its legally binding obligations under the NPT. We urge Iran to work with the IAEA towards full compliance with its comprehensive safeguards agreement and immediately enable the resumption of the Agency's verification activities. A lasting solution to the Iranian nuclear issue must be sought by diplomatic means. The nuclear and missile programs of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, which violate multiple UN Security Council resolutions, remain a threat to regional and international peace and security. The DPRK can never have the status of a nuclear weapons state and must abandon its illegal nuclear and missile programs in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner. The Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty is an integral part of the nuclear arms control architecture. We reiterate our call on all states that have not yet signed or ratified the treaty to do so without further delay, and we demand all states to abide by a moratorium on nuclear test explosions. The Nordic countries are deeply concerned by China's rapid expansion of its nuclear arsenal. We urge China to engage in meaningful dialogue on arms control, confidence building and transparency measures regarding its nuclear capabilities. The New START Treaty serves an important stabilizing role, contributes to confidence building and risk reduction. We regret Russia's so-called suspension of the treaty and call for the urgent commencement of negotiations for a successor agreement. We strongly encourage China to join such negotiations. Termination of fissile material production and eradication of existing stocks are essential steps in nuclear disarmament. We reaffirm our support for the commencement of negotiations on a fissile material cut-off treaty. We encourage all States to support the establishment of a group of scientific and technical experts on nuclear disarmament verification. Mr. Chair, The Nordic countries will continue to promote the full and effective implementation of the Biological Weapons Convention and Chemical Weapons Convention and defend the norm against the use of biological and chemical weapons. We condemn Russia's use of riot control agents as a method of warfare in Ukraine, explicitly prohibited under the CWC. and remain deeply concerned by the use of choking agent chloropicrin against Ukrainian soldiers. We demand that Russia comply with its obligations. Any use of chemical weapons is contrary to international law and accountability for violations must be ensured. We underline our full support for the work of the OPCW and our confidence in the technical secretariat. This year marked the 100th anniversary of the Geneva Protocol and the 50th anniversary of the Biological Weapons Convention. We are encouraged by the deliberations of the Working Group on the Strengthening of the BWC and encourage all parties to remain engaged in these efforts. We underline that multilateral export control regimes are important elements of the non-proliferation architecture and serve to facilitate international cooperation on peaceful uses of technology. Mr. Chair, the Nordic countries are consistent supporters of instruments addressing the illicit flow of small arms and light weapons. We call for the universalization of the Arms Trade Treaty and warmly welcome the recent decision to elaborate a five-year strategy for ATT. The Nordic countries remain firmly committed to the humanitarian objectives of the Anti-Personnel Landmine Convention. Despite Finland's announcement regarding its withdrawal, all Nordic countries continue to recognize and support the Convention's vital role in advancing global efforts to reduce the use of anti-personnel landmines and mitigate their humanitarian impact. We continue to contribute substantially to global humanitarian mine action efforts. The use of explosive weapons in populated areas poses great risk to civilians and civilian infrastructure. We encourage states to endorse the EWIPA political declaration, which aims to strengthen the protection of civilians. We also highlight the continued relevance of Security Council Resolution 1325 and subsequent resolutions that address the impact of armed conflict on women and the importance of the full and equal participation in peace and security processes. Mr. Chair, the international community must keep pace with the rapid development of emerging and disruptive technologies and shape standards and principles to ensure the responsible use in accordance with international law. The Nordic countries support the work of the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems under the CCW. We find the chair's rolling text to be a sufficient basis to move towards negotiations of an instrument on laws at the CCW once the GGE mandate expires next year. We also welcome the diverse multi-stakeholder discussions and initiatives on the responsible use of artificial intelligence in the military domain and emphasize the need to keep these efforts complementary and inclusive. The Nordic countries have firmly committed to the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. We support the continued work of the open-ended working group on PAROS and look forward to continued discussions in the UN on the development of norms, rules and principles of responsible behaviour in outer space. We urge all states to abide by the Outer Space Treaty. Mr. Chair, in closing, we look forward to further deliberations on the UNAT initiative, including in the context of arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation. The Nordic countries will continue to make every effort to advance the important work of this committee. Thank you.
I thank her Excellency, Permanent Representative of Iceland, and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kuwait on behalf of the Gulf Cooperation Council.

In the name of God, most gracious, most merciful. This interlinkage between the standing of the UN and the protection of civilians in conflicts leads me to address the risks of broader escalation in the region. Concerns about the Iranian nuclear file must be addressed exclusively through peaceful and diplomatic means. We support diplomatic solutions and welcome ongoing regional and international efforts to revive negotiations and address concerns promoting regional security and stability. We commend the tireless efforts of the Sultanate of Oman in creating a climate conducive for dialogue. We commend the constructive role of Egypt in reaching the Cairo understandings on the resumption of cooperation between Iran and the IAEA. We warn that the erosion of trust in the effectiveness of international treaties and questioning their effectiveness weaken collective regime and multilateral system. reiterate that the proliferation of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction is one of the gravest threats to international peace and security. Strict adherence to relevant international treaties, mainly the NPT, is critical to addressing these concerns. In this context, We underscore the vital importance of establishing a zone free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in the Middle East. This is an essential step to ensuring lasting security and stability. This goal was and remains an integral part of the 1995 indefinite extension package of the NPT. Any procrastination in implementing this resolution and the outcome document of the 2010 review conference undermines the credibility of the non-proliferation architecture. We call on the international community to shoulder its responsibilities and to pressure Israel to comply with international law. Israel must accede to the NPT and must place its nuclear facilities under the IAEA comprehensive safeguards regime. Israel is the only party in the region that possesses a nuclear weapon without international control and oversight. We welcome the five sessions of the conference for the establishment of the free zone in accordance with General Assembly Resolution 546/73. We welcome efforts during Mauritania's presidency of the fifth session. We welcome the outcomes reached. We look forward to the upcoming sixth session to be presided by Morocco in November. We hope that this session will bring parties closer, leading to a legally binding instrument. We call on all parties to engage in the session. We look forward to the success of the next review NPT conference after the past two conferences have failed to reach consensus results. The States Parties must shoulder their responsibility to ensure the credibility of the regime. Chair, we are deeply concerned over the continued qualitative and quantitative development by some nuclear weapon states of their arsenal in violation of the NPT. This entrenches double standards and undermines collective efforts for complete nuclear disarmament for the furtherance of international peace and security. reiterate that the scope of the Conference on Disarmament must be broadened. The Conference must be empowered to fulfill its negotiating mandate, being the negotiating body on disarmament. The current deadlock is due to lack of political will by some countries, not to institutional deficiencies. Chair, the illicit proliferation of conventional weapons, mainly small arms and light weapons, that foment and prolong conflict is no less dangerous. We call for stronger international cooperation in controlling and regulating the circulation of these weapons. Technical assistance must be provided to countries wishing to develop their control regimes to ensure that these weapons are exclusively used by states and their legitimate services. We reject any attempts to impose obligations on contentious issues that do not enjoy international consensus or attempts to restrict the legitimate right of states to self-defense in accordance with the UN Charter. On cybersecurity, we congratulate Singapore on the successful conclusion of the OEWG on the security of and the use of ICT 2021-2025. We welcome the consensus adoption of the final report on 11 July 2025. This paved the way for a UN permanent mechanism to pursue discussions on responsible state behavior in cyberspace. We welcome the leading and constructive role of His Excellency Ambassador Burhan Ghaffur. Chair, we reiterate that outer space must be preserved exclusively for peaceful uses. We call for efforts to prevent the militarization of outer space. We must prevent an arms race in outer space. International cooperation must be promoted to ensure safe and sustainable use of outer space to serve the interests of all countries and promote international peace and security. Chair. reiterate that our solidarity is a safety valve for regional security and stability. Any attack against any GCC country is in its essence an attack on all GCC countries. We will perceive any such attack as a collective threat that requires deterrence and retaliation. The Gulf national security is not open for adventures or gambles. It is rather a red line that must not be crossed. GCC countries have long exercised self-restraint and called for peaceful solutions. We reiterate that we will not be complacent in the future with any attempt to undermine our security. Gulf security will continue to serve as a shield against threats to defend our peoples and to promote international peace and security. In conclusion, Mr. Chair, Addressing disarmament and non-proliferation challenges requires collective commitment from all parties who pursue our constructive cooperation with the U.N. and all partners for a more stable and balanced international order, for a fairer international order that can end nuclear threats and restore international law as an inclusive frame of reference. This will guarantee our people's legitimate right to peace, development, and stability. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kuwait. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt on behalf of the New Agenda Coalition. Please.

Thank you, Chair, Chairperson, Under-Secretary-General High Representative Nakamitsu, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honor to take the floor on behalf of the members of the New Agenda Coalition, namely Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, South Africa, and my own country, Egypt. At the outset, the New Agenda Coalition congratulates Your Excellency, Ambassador Maurizio Massari, on your assumption as chair of this year's first committee. We assure you of the next support. Chair, we meet today as we honor the 80th anniversary of the United Nations. In 1946, the General Assembly unanimously adopted its very first resolution, which established a commission to make proposals for the elimination from national armaments of atomic weapons and all other major weapons adaptable to mass destruction. Unfortunately, this ambition has not been realized. The NAC is a cross-regional group of non-nuclear weapon states united in their common goal of achieving the total elimination of nuclear weapons. the very same goal as presented in the very first resolution adopted by the UNGA 80 years ago. In advancing the globally shared objective of a nuclear weapon-free world, our coalition is fully committed to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the cornerstone of disarmament and non-proliferation regime, and its three pillars, nuclear disarmament, nuclear non-proliferation, and the peaceful uses of nuclear energy. The NAC believes that nuclear disarmament and nuclear non-proliferation are mutually reinforcing processes. The NAC reaffirms that the only guarantee against the use, threat of use, or further proliferation of nuclear weapons is their total elimination. The current global peace and security challenges have resulted in profound nuclear dangers. Many current conflicts involve a nuclear dimension, including in the Middle East and Europe, and there are heightened tensions in North East and South Asia, as well implicit and explicit threats of nuclear weapon use. Unfortunately, we still remain far from achieving the ultimate goal of a world free from nuclear weapons that we all aspire to. On the contrary, it is deeply alarming that nuclear weapons states have not made meaningful progress on their unequivocal undertaking to accomplish the total elimination of their nuclear weapons arsenals under the NPT's Article VI. The NAC recalls the treaty was never intended to create an entitlement for some states to possess nuclear weapons indefinitely. The NAC does not accept the argument that improvements in the international security environment should be a precondition for disarmament. Any presumption by nuclear weapons states for indefinite possession of nuclear weapons is contrary not only to the grand bargain upon which the NPT was founded, but also to the decision on the treaty's indefinite extension in 1995. The indefinite retention or acquisition of nuclear weapons does not enhance international peace and security. Rather, nuclear weapons detract from ensuring sustainable international peace and security, irrespective of whose hands they are in. Chair, the NAC is deeply concerned by continuous actions that weaken the disarmament and non-proliferation architecture and undermine key norms. Likewise, by the dismantling of core agreements among nuclear weapon states, including the Intermediate Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, INF, the Open Skies Treaty, and the suspension of the Treaty for Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms, New START Treaty. the only remaining bilateral arms control agreement between the United States and Russia, which is set to expire on February 5, 2026. We encourage both parties to the New START Treaty to resume its full and effective implementation, to ensure current limits are not abandoned, and to urgently negotiate a successor agreement. While the NAC welcomes the positive and important role of certain measures such as those that aim at reducing nuclear risk, the NAC reaffirms they are of a complementary nature and should not be considered as a substitute or as a prerequisite for nuclear disarmament. The NAC remains profoundly concerned by policies and pronouncements that diverge from the shared objective of achieving the total elimination of nuclear weapons. We remain concerned by longstanding inertia regarding ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, CDTB, by nuclear weapon states and recent moves to withdraw ratification. Any indications of a retreat from longstanding commitments to nuclear testing moratoria or to the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty are troubling at a time when the treaty's relevance is greater than ever. These dynamics have been preventing the entry into force of the treaty, and so there remains the risk that nuclear testing could resume. The NAC remains deeply alarmed by the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of any use of nuclear weapons, which would transcend national borders and for which no state has adequate response capacity. The NAC welcomes the positive development that the successful convening of the third meeting of states parties to the TPNW The TPNW is fully consistent with the NPT and is complementary to its legal obligations. Both treaties offer a sound and mutually reinforcing legal framework for nuclear disarmament. The NAC is further concerned about unpredictable new strategic factors involving developments in the field of outer space, artificial intelligence and cyberspace, which have the potential to increase the risk of use or threat of use of nuclear weapons. The coalition welcomes transparency measures undertaken by some nuclear weapon states and calls for increased measures from all such states. The NAC stresses that transparency is an intrinsic element for accountability on nuclear weapon states' disarmament obligations and commitments. Chair, the NAC reaffirms the significant contribution of nuclear weapon free zones to nuclear disarmament efforts and achieving a nuclear weapon free world. The NAC encourages nuclear weapon states that have not yet done so to sign and ratify the protocols to these treaties and to withdraw any reservations or interpretive declarations thereto. The NAC emphasizes the importance of the full implementation of the 1995 resolution on the Middle East on the establishment of a zone free of nuclear weapons and all other weapons of mass destruction. The NAC acknowledges the successful organization by the United Nations Secretary General since 2019 over the five sessions of a conference, the last of which in 2025, to elaborate a treaty to establish the zone on the basis of arrangements freely arrived at by all the states of the region. And we are encouraged by the outcomes. We should capitalize on the progress achieved so far. Chair, for more than a decade and a half, NPT review conferences have failed to adopt an outcome document. The NAC regrets the failure to adopt a final document at the 2022 review conference. Despite the hope among states following the successful adoption of the 2010 Action Plan, including the 22 actions on nuclear disarmament, 15 years later, we remain far from advancing implementation of this plan. The 2010 Action Plan, as well as the decisions adopted at the 1995 Review Conference and the 13 practical steps agreed in 2000, remain valid and must be implemented, in particular by nuclear weapon states. A lack of concrete steps towards nuclear disarmament by nuclear weapon states has endangered the credibility of the nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime founded upon the NPT. The NAC is fully committed to the success of the upcoming NPT review conference in 2026, a critical juncture for the regime. The NAC urges all NPT states parties, in particular, NWS, to do their outmost to this end. The NAC also regrets the continued failure of the Conference on Disarmament to fulfill its negotiating mandate for nearly three decades. The protracted failure of the nuclear disarmament machinery is reflective of the crisis and challenges this regime is facing. Mr. Chairperson, almost 30 years ago, the NAC Ministers of Foreign Affairs called on the governments of each of the nuclear weapons states and the then nuclear weapons capable states that have not yet acceded to the NPT to commit themselves unequivocally to their total elimination. of the respective nuclear weapons and nuclear weapons capability and agree to start working immediately on the practical steps and negotiations required for its achievement. This call remains valid and will continue to be until it is achieved. As we approach the 11th Review Conference, there is a clear and urgent need for all States Parties to the NPT to confront the challenges facing the Treaty. This would require our united resolve and concrete steps towards the full implementation of the NPT's Article VI obligations, fundamentally by the nuclear weapon states. Nuclear weapons continue to occupy a central role in the security doctrines of nuclear weapon states and those under extended nuclear security guarantees, placing the collective well-being of all states and people at continued risk. As long as nuclear weapons states continue to defer their obligations, and while increasing the salience of nuclear deterrence in security doctrines, policies and plans, the Treaty risks losing its value as a significant contributor to international peace and security, with a direct negative impact on nuclear non-proliferation efforts. All states must resist these trends, as the demise of the Treaty would have negative effects for our common security. In today's world, the NPT remains irreplaceable. It provides the order for our international disarmament and non-proliferation regime. To halt the erosion of the NPT and ensure its long-term viability, the nuclear weapon states must show real leadership between now and next year's review conference. Collectively, we must uphold the integrity of the treaty so as to help achieve our shared goal of a world free of nuclear weapons. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
